cards.title: Commit Log Architecture, Topics, Partitions & Offsets
cards.question: Explain Commit Log Architecture, Topics, Partitions & Offsets
cards.answer_30s: Kafka is a distributed, append-only commit log. Topics are split into ordered, immutable Partitions spread across brokers; each record within a partition gets a sequential 64-bit Offset. Consumers track their own offsets, allowing independent replay and multiple consumer groups reading at different speeds.
cards.typical_use: Event-driven microservices, CDC pipelines, and high-throughput telemetry.
pitfalls: Strict ordering is guaranteed ONLY within a single partition, never across partitions.

cards.title: Producers: acks, Retries & Idempotent Delivery
cards.question: Explain Producers: acks, Retries & Idempotent Delivery
cards.answer_30s: `acks=0` (fire-and-forget), `acks=1` (leader wrote), `acks=all` (-1, all In-Sync Replicas wrote). Enabling `enable.idempotence=true` assigns producer IDs and sequence numbers so broker retries never create duplicate records on network blips.

cards.title: Consumer Groups & Cooperative Sticky Rebalancing
cards.question: Explain Consumer Groups & Cooperative Sticky Rebalancing
cards.answer_30s: Within a Consumer Group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer instance, capping max parallelism at the partition count. CooperativeStickyAssignor performs incremental rebalances without stop-the-world pauses across unaffected partitions.
cards.typical_use: Scaling consumers horizontally without losing per-key ordering.
pitfalls: Disable `enable.auto.commit` and commit offsets manually AFTER downstream DB/API writes succeed.

cards.title: Zero-Copy (sendfile), OS Page Cache & Batching
cards.question: Explain Zero-Copy (sendfile), OS Page Cache & Batching
cards.answer_30s: Kafka achieves massive throughput by appending sequentially to disk and relying on the Linux OS Page Cache instead of JVM heap. When serving consumers, `sendfile()` transfers bytes directly from kernel page cache to NIC socket buffer with zero user-space copies.
cards.typical_use: Streaming millions of events per second on commodity hardware.
pitfalls: Batching (`linger.ms` + `batch.size`) + `lz4`/`zstd` compression drastically cuts broker CPU and network I/O.

cards.title: ISR, Leader Election & Unclean Leader Election
cards.question: Explain ISR, Leader Election & Unclean Leader Election
cards.answer_30s: Each partition has one leader (handles all reads/writes) and N-1 followers. Followers staying caught up form the In-Sync Replicas (ISR) set. Keeping `unclean.leader.election.enable=false` prevents an out-of-sync follower from becoming leader and silently dropping committed data.
cards.typical_use: Preventing split-brain data loss during broker hardware failures.
pitfalls: If fewer than `min.insync.replicas` are alive, `acks=all` producers fail fast with NotEnoughReplicasException rather than risking data loss.

cards.title: Retry Topics, Dead Letter Queues (DLQ) & Poison Pills
cards.question: Explain Retry Topics, Dead Letter Queues (DLQ) & Poison Pills
cards.answer_30s: Blocking a consumer thread on a failing poison-pill message stalls the entire partition. Production consumers route transient errors to exponential-backoff retry topics and permanent schema/business failures to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) before advancing the offset.
cards.typical_use: Keeping streaming pipelines unblocked when malformed events arrive.
pitfalls: Preserve original headers (error reason, stacktrace, retry count, original offset) in DLQ records for replay.

cards.title: Schema Registry & Evolution (Avro / Protobuf)
cards.question: Explain Schema Registry & Evolution (Avro / Protobuf)
cards.answer_30s: Schema Registry stores versioned schemas outside message payloads, embedding only a 4-byte schema ID per record. Enforcing BACKWARD or FULL compatibility prevents producers from breaking downstream consumers on schema changes.

pitfalls: Prefer Avro or Protobuf over raw JSON for compact wire size and strict contract enforcement.

cards.title: Q: Why can't you have more active consumers than partitions in a group?
cards.question: Q: Why can't you have more active consumers than partitions in a group?
cards.answer_30s: A: Because Kafka guarantees ordered processing by assigning each partition to at most one consumer in a group. Extra consumers sit idle as hot standbys. To scale beyond current partition count, increase partitions (note: changing partition count alters hash(key) % N routing).
pitfalls: Over-partitioning too aggressively increases open file handles, metadata overhead, and failover time—aim for balanced partition counts.

cards.title: Q: What causes Consumer Lag and how do you diagnose/fix it?
cards.question: Q: What causes Consumer Lag and how do you diagnose/fix it?
cards.answer_30s: A: Consumer lag = Log-End Offset minus Committed Offset. Diagnose by checking: 1) Slow downstream DB/API sinks, 2) Frequent rebalance storms (`max.poll.interval.ms` exceeded), 3) Hot partition key skew, or 4) Under-provisioned consumers. Fix by batching sink writes, tuning `max.poll.records`, fixing partition keys, or scaling consumers.
cards.typical_use: Most common Kafka production debugging interview question.
pitfalls: If `max.poll.interval.ms` is exceeded during slow processing, the broker kicks the consumer out, triggering endless rebalances.

cards.title: Q: How does Kafka achieve Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS)?
cards.question: Q: How does Kafka achieve Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS)?
cards.answer_30s: A: EOS combines three pieces: 1) Idempotent producers (`enable.idempotence=true`) to prevent broker duplicates, 2) Kafka Transactions (`initTransactions`, `sendOffsetsToTransaction`) for atomic read-process-write across Kafka topics, and 3) Idempotent/transactional writes when sinking to external DBs (e.g. upsert by event_id).

pitfalls: Always clarify: Kafka transactions only cover Kafka-to-Kafka; external DBs still need idempotency keys!

cards.title: Q: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS — when do you choose Kafka?
cards.question: Q: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS — when do you choose Kafka?
cards.answer_30s: A: Choose Kafka for high-throughput event streaming, event sourcing, multiple independent consumer groups, and replayable retention logs. Choose RabbitMQ/SQS for traditional task queues with per-message ACKs, complex routing exchanges, or delayed/priority jobs where messages are deleted once processed.

code.body: # Kafka = durable replayable log | RabbitMQ/SQS = smart broker, destructive queue

pitfalls: Note Kafka's pull-based consumer model allows consumers to control their own backpressure rate.

cards.title: Q: What is Log Compaction and when do you use it?
cards.question: Q: What is Log Compaction and when do you use it?
cards.answer_30s: A: Standard retention deletes segments by time or size. Log compaction (`cleanup.policy=compact`) retains at least the latest value for every message key indefinitely, acting like a changelog table for stateful caches, CDC, or user profile snapshots.
cards.typical_use: Rebuilding service state or materialized views from a Kafka topic.
pitfalls: Send a `null` value (tombstone) for a key to delete it during compaction.

cards.title: Q: What is a Hot Partition and how do you fix it?
cards.question: Q: What is a Hot Partition and how do you fix it?
cards.answer_30s: A: If a high-volume key (e.g. `merchant_id=amazon` or `null` in older clients) hashes to one partition, that partition and its consumer get overloaded while others sit idle. Fix by choosing a higher-cardinality composite key (`merchant_id:shard_0..9`) or round-robin when strict global entity ordering isn't required.

code.body: # Composite key distributes load across 10 partitions while keeping sub-shard order

cards.typical_use: Practical skew mitigation in streaming systems.
pitfalls: Mention that Kafka 2.4+'s StickyPartitioner batches key-less records efficiently instead of pure round-robin.

cards.title: Q: What is the Outbox Pattern with Kafka (CDC / Debezium)?
cards.question: Q: What is the Outbox Pattern with Kafka (CDC / Debezium)?
cards.answer_30s: A: Writing to PostgreSQL and publishing to Kafka in two separate calls can fail halfway (dual-write problem). Instead, insert the domain row AND an outbox event row in the SAME local DB transaction, then let Debezium stream the DB WAL/outbox table reliably to Kafka.

code.body: BEGIN; INSERT INTO orders ...; INSERT INTO outbox_events ...; COMMIT;

cards.typical_use: Guaranteeing atomic state + event publication without 2PC.
pitfalls: This is the industry-standard solution to the dual-write consistency problem.

cards.title: Q: How does KRaft replace ZooKeeper in modern Kafka?
cards.question: Q: How does KRaft replace ZooKeeper in modern Kafka?
cards.answer_30s: A: Historically Kafka used ZooKeeper for cluster metadata, controller election, and topic configs, creating two systems to operate. KRaft embeds a Raft consensus quorum directly inside Kafka brokers, enabling faster controller failover and scaling to millions of partitions.
